tagline.text: Bacolod's pick-your-own seafood market with cook-it-for-you stalls

location.label: Location
location.text: Corner of San Juan Street and North Capitol Road, Bacolod City (behind the Provincial Capitol)

children.text: Old Pala-Pala is a seafood market on the back streets behind the Bacolod provincial capitol. Buy fish, shrimp or squid at the market, hand it to a nearby tulahan (cook-for-you eatery), and they will prepare it on the spot. It works like Manila's dampa, but is more modest and cheaper.

Pala-pala is the local name for a seafood market in Bacolod, and Old Pala-Pala sits right behind the Negros Occidental Provincial Capitol, at the corner of San Juan Street and North Capitol Road. It is about a
10–15 minute
walk from the Capitol Park and Lagoon, or roughly
by tricycle from the lagoon, so it pairs well with a visit to
Negros Occidental Provincial Capitol and Lagoon

The heart of the place is paluto, meaning you buy the food and have it cooked for you. Choose fish, shrimp, squid, scallops or crab at the market stalls, then take them to one of the small eateries called tulahan lining the area, and they will cook them any way you like. Some tulahan will even buy the seafood from the market for you, so travelers who are shy about picking or bargaining can relax. It is the same idea as Manila's dampa.

The atmosphere is far from polished restaurant rows. Many places are plain, with plastic chairs, formica tables, bamboo walls and shared sinks, and when the evening fish market gets going, the catch is piled up under bare light bulbs. Freshness and price are what people have praised for years. A newer, tidier pala-pala also exists on the 18th Street side of the city, and the old market is described as the more budget-friendly of the two.

Two tulahan that blogs mention often are Hyksos Tulahan and Nening's Tulahan. A 2011–2012 review of the first reported a meal of shrimp and scallops on a budget of ₱150~350 per person, and a 2016 review of the second described a spread of squid, lobster, shrimp and grilled blue marlin for about ₱570, with cooking charged at around ₱90 per dish. Whether those places are still there, and what they charge now, you will need to check on site. Most detailed reviews of this market date from roughly 2011–2016, so shops and prices may have changed since. Treat every amount below as approximate and confirm prices locally.
Take what you chose at the market to a tulahan and they will cook it for a cooking fee based on the style. The same ingredients can be grilled, made into soup, or done in butter, among other options.

Tilapia, lapu-lapu (grouper), blue marlin, tuna, bangus (milkfish), squid, sea prawns, lobster, crab, scallops and oysters are among the items mentioned. What is available depends on the day's catch, so walk the stalls and see.
A dish that reviews mention again and again is blue marlin grilled with soy sauce and calamansi. The thick flesh eats like a steak.
Garlic-butter scallops, garlic shrimp, chili crab and squid calamares are popular orders at almost any tulahan.
Fish soup made as tinola (a ginger broth) and fish grilled over charcoal, called sinugba, go well with rice. They are the safest choices for tasting the local flavor.
The market is liveliest in the late afternoon, when the catch is delivered to wholesalers. Watching the haggling under bare bulbs is part of the fun.
The provincial capitol and lagoon park are within walking distance, so it is easy to plan a day of the park by day and pala-pala in the evening.

Facing the market there is also a proper restaurant where you order from a menu. It suits anyone who feels awkward choosing ingredients or wants a more formal setting, and it is said not to be expensive.

items.title: Evening paluto route
items.subtitle: Lagoon stroll, then a seafood dinner

children.text: Walk around Capitol Lagoon Park and feed the fish. The park has the capitol building and carabao sculptures.
Walk about
10–15 minutes
from the lagoon to Old Pala-Pala. The late afternoon, when the fish market is on, is the best time to pick fresh ingredients.
Make a lap of the stalls, compare prices, and choose the fish, shrimp and squid you like. Have them weighed and confirm the price first.
Hand the ingredients to a tulahan and tell them how you want them cooked. Ordering two or three styles, such as grilled, soup and garlic butter, to share works well.
Finish your meal, pay, and head back to your hotel by tricycle, jeepney or Grab.

Cooking can take a while, so leave plenty of time for the meal. With two or three people or more you can share several dishes, and the cost per person drops. Bring an umbrella if it rains and eat under a shop's roof. After dinner, a slow walk back toward the lagoon park is a nice way to end the evening.

Come back into the city and rest at the lagoon park.
Buy seafood at Old Pala-Pala and finish the day with dinner.
Walk in from the San Juan Street side behind the capitol and browse the stalls at the market entrance. If you ask the names of the fish and shells on offer, the vendors tend to be happy to explain.
Compare the menus and cooking fees at two or three tulahan, and have a look at the formal restaurant in front of the market too.
Hand over just one small item, such as squid calamares or garlic-butter scallops, taste it and leave.
If you are short on time, you can just have a taste like this and come back for a proper meal another day.

If you take a taxi or Grab, tell the driver San Juan Street behind the Provincial Capitol. The capitol is the easiest landmark.
Jeepney routes and fares can change, so confirm with the driver before you board.
The market runs year-round, and its hours are listed as 8:00 AM to 10:00 PM daily, though individual stalls may differ. Fresh catch tends to arrive in the late afternoon, so early evening is best.

In Bacolod the wet season runs from May to December, with the heaviest rain in August and September, and January to April is relatively dry. There are covered shops, so you can still eat in the rain, but rough seas can reduce the catch. During the October MassKara Festival the city gets very crowded, so secure lodging and a table in advance.
Evenings bring more customers and you may have to wait for a table, so it is more relaxed to go early, choose your ingredients and grab a seat.

There is little lodging around Old Pala-Pala, so the usual approach is to stay at a hotel in central Bacolod and drop by in the evening. Several hotels are found around the capitol and lagoon park and along Lacson Street. When choosing a hotel, it helps to check that the market is within tricycle distance.

There is also a formal restaurant in front of the market, so if choosing and handing over your own ingredients feels like too much, you can simply order from the menu there. Bacolod is famous for dishes such as chicken inasal, piaya and cansi, so mix them with the seafood to vary your meals through the day.

This is a place better suited to dinner than lunch. Reviews also recommend the late afternoon, when the fresh catch comes in. If you are in a big group, it is best to secure a table first and then shop. If choosing ingredients is difficult, tell the tulahan staff your budget and ask them to choose for you. According to reviews, the staff will then buy them from the stalls on your behalf.
Go in the late afternoon to pick freshly arrived ingredients.
Do not look at only one tulahan. Compare prices at two or three stalls before choosing.
When buying, check the weight with your own eyes and ask the price first to avoid arguments later.
Cooking fees vary with the style and ingredients, so ask for the total before you hand anything over.
Go with two or three people or more and share several dishes. That is the most economical way.
If it is your first time, do not hand everything to one place. Order a single dish first, see the taste and the cooking fee, and then order more.
Mix styles, such as one grilled dish, one soup and one fried dish, so you do not get tired of it.
Bring plenty of small bills and coins, and ask the shop whether cards are accepted.
The smell of seafood can cling to clothes, so wear something comfortable.
Before you go, check the address (San Juan Street) and the latest reviews on Google Maps, and ask the shop whether it takes cards or only cash.
Most reviews are old, so shops and prices may have changed. Check recent Google Maps reviews before you go.
If you hand over food for cooking without confirming the weight and price, the price may end up different later, so always confirm first.
Seafood spoils easily. Judge freshness by sight and smell, and eat only fully cooked food.
If you are allergic to shellfish or crustaceans, tell the shop before ordering.
The market lanes are crowded, so keep valuables secure, and use Grab or a taxi late at night.
Do not confuse this with the newer Pala-Pala market or the 18th Street market. Make sure you are at San Juan Street behind the Provincial Capitol.
Opening hours differ by shop, and some may close on holidays or in heavy rain. Check the latest information.
